stories.headline: Pierre Poilievre to travel to Washington to advocate for tariff-free trade
stories.summary: Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre is scheduled to visit Washington next week to meet with American officials and lobby against proposed U.S. tariffs on Canadian goods. The trip comes as federal ministers continue bilateral negotiations to protect cross-border supply chains. Poilievre's office notified the Prime Minister's Office of the travel plans and will receive a briefing from Canada's ambassador to the United States.

stories.headline: Supreme Court largely upholds Quebec secularism law and use of notwithstanding clause
stories.summary: The Supreme Court of Canada has largely upheld Quebec's Bill 21, ruling that provincial governments can pre-emptively invoke the Charter's notwithstanding clause to shield legislation from court challenges, though it invalidated provisions applying to elected members of the National Assembly. The decision cements the ban on religious symbols for public servants in positions of authority, including teachers and police officers. While Quebec leaders welcomed the confirmation of provincial autonomy, civil liberties groups, affected workers, and other provincial leaders condemned the law as discriminatory.

stories.headline: Prime Minister Mark Carney to whip Liberal caucus vote on major projects legislation
stories.summary: Prime Minister Mark Carney announced that all Liberal MPs will be required to vote in favour of Bill C-39, legislation intended to expedite federal regulatory approvals for major industrial projects and overhaul parts of the Canada Labour Code. The decision to whip the vote ensures the contested bill's passage through the House of Commons despite internal debate and criticism from opposition parties. The move comes shortly after the government House leader described the legislation as a straightforward priority.

stories.headline: Ottawa adds Mackenzie Valley Highway to federal list of national interest projects
stories.summary: The federal government has officially designated the proposed 800-kilometre Mackenzie Valley Highway in the Northwest Territories as a project of national interest to accelerate its construction. Prime Minister Mark Carney and N.W.T. Premier R.J. Simpson stated the year-round road will enhance Arctic security, improve transportation reliability for remote communities, and unlock critical resource extraction opportunities. The project marks the first major northern infrastructure development fast-tracked under the federal designation.

stories.headline: Ottawa launches 6.5-billion-dollar national strategy to modernize Canadian forestry
stories.summary: The federal government has unveiled a $6.5-billion national forestry strategy intended to revitalize an industry hit by decades of economic challenges and trade barriers. The plan aims to transition producers away from traditional lumber and pulp towards high-value advanced wood products and sustainable technologies by 2050. British Columbia officials and industry stakeholders welcomed the investment as an essential move to restore global competitiveness.

stories.headline: CRTC orders Bell, Rogers, and Telus to eliminate prohibited wireless fees
stories.summary: The Canadian Radio-television and Telecommunications Commission has ruled that Bell, Rogers, and Telus violated federal regulations by charging customers prohibited fees under the Telecommunications Act. The regulator ordered all three telecom giants to cease billing the disputed charges by December 27. The enforcement action is aimed at cracking down on deceptive junk fees across Canadian mobile plans.

stories.headline: British Columbia court rules faith-based hospitals can prohibit medical assistance in dying
stories.summary: The British Columbia Supreme Court has upheld provincial policies permitting denominational health-care facilities to refuse to provide medical assistance in dying on site. The court ruled that requiring patients to transfer to other institutions does not infringe on their constitutional right to access MAID. The decision, arising from a challenge at Vancouver's St. Paul's Hospital, has prompted grief and anger from affected families and advocates seeking unhindered end-of-life care across Canada.

stories.headline: Federal government shortlists seven design and construction teams to renovate 24 Sussex
stories.summary: Public Services and Procurement Canada has selected seven teams of architects and builders for the design competition to rehabilitate 24 Sussex Drive. The historic official residence of the prime minister has been uninhabitable for years due to deteriorating infrastructure and mechanical systems. The federal government anticipates selecting the winning team by July 2027 to restore the residence.

stories.headline: Ontario urges federal government to strengthen Criminal Code protections for home invasion victims
stories.summary: Ontario Attorney General Doug Downey and Solicitor General Michael Kerzner have sent a letter urging Ottawa to clarify and strengthen self-defence protections under the Criminal Code for homeowners confronting intruders. The request follows a wave of violent home invasions in the Greater Toronto Area and controversial remarks by Premier Doug Ford suggesting residents defend themselves. Legal experts and critics caution that ambiguous self-defence laws risk dangerous vigilantism while proponents argue victims need greater legal clarity.

stories.headline: Crown seeks 25 years for Kenneth Law after apology to victims' families
stories.summary: At a sentencing hearing in Ontario, prosecutors requested a 25-year prison term for Kenneth Law, who pleaded guilty to 14 counts of aiding suicide after selling lethal sodium nitrite packages online worldwide. Law addressed the court and apologized directly to the victims' families, admitting that his online business was categorically wrong. The defence and Crown presented sharply contrasting sentencing recommendations as the court considers his culpability in dozens of related deaths.

stories.headline: Ontario government reviews online gambling regulations amid backlash over aggressive advertising
stories.summary: Ontario Gaming Minister Zee Hamid announced that the province is reviewing its online sports betting framework and considering tighter restrictions on advertisements in the new year. The move follows Premier Doug Ford's public criticism that gambling commercials have become out of control across Ontario broadcasts and digital platforms. Hamid confirmed the province is exploring every option to mitigate potential harms and rein in excessive promotional campaigns.

stories.headline: Release of revised Alto high-speed rail corridor delayed until January amid rural concerns
stories.summary: The federal Alto high-speed rail project between Toronto and Quebec City has postponed the release of its revised track corridor until January. Rural communities and property owners along the proposed route have organized protests over potential expropriations and disruption to agricultural land. The planned 1,000-kilometre electrified passenger rail line continues to face intense public scrutiny regarding route selection and property rights.

stories.headline: Ontario teachers warn of escalating grade inflation in for-profit private high schools
stories.summary: Ontario educators are raising alarms that the province's proliferation of for-profit private schools has created an unmonitored market for inflated grades. Teachers report that students are increasingly obtaining distorted course marks that bypass traditional academic standards to gain competitive university admissions. The trend has intensified calls for the Ministry of Education to strengthen inspection and accreditation oversight of private credit mills.

stories.headline: Glendon College rejects proposal to move programs to York University's Keele campus
stories.summary: The Faculty Council of Glendon College has decisively rejected a proposal to relocate the bilingual liberal arts institution from its midtown Toronto campus to York University's main Keele campus. Faculty voted 61 to 8 against the administration's consolidation plan, demanding that the university instead invest in revitalizing the historic campus. The vote protects the unique standalone identity of southern Ontario's premier bilingual post-secondary institution.

stories.headline: City of Toronto reviews municipal credit cards following unauthorized staff purchases
stories.summary: Scrutiny has emerged at Toronto City Hall over employee credit card expenditures, with records revealing purchases on personal items including dating apps, concert tickets, and sports games. The questionable charges on city-issued corporate cards have raised concerns over spending oversight and internal controls among municipal staff. The city is facing calls to tighten approval processes and recover misspent public funds.
